name: To Go Or Not To Go?
description: Dima overslept the alarm clock, which was supposed to raise him to school. Dima wonders if he will have time to come to the first lesson. To do this, he needs to know the minimum time it will take him to get from home to school. The city where Dima lives is a rectangular field of $$$n \times m$$$ size. Each cell $$$(i, j)$$$ on this field is denoted by one number $$$a_{ij}$$$: The number $$$-1$$$ means that the passage through the cell is prohibited; The number $$$0$$$ means that the cell is free and Dima can walk though it. The number $$$x$$$ ($$$1 \le x \le 10^9$$$) means that the cell contains a portal with a cost of $$$x$$$. A cell with a portal is also considered free. From any portal, Dima can go to any other portal, while the time of moving from the portal $$$(i, j)$$$ to the portal $$$(x, y)$$$ corresponds to the sum of their costs $$$a_{ij} + a_{xy}$$$. In addition to moving between portals, Dima can also move between unoccupied cells adjacent to one side in time $$$w$$$. In particular, he can enter a cell with a portal and not use it. Initially, Dima is in the upper-left cell $$$(1, 1)$$$, and the school is in the lower right cell $$$(n, m)$$$.
input_specification: The first line contains three integers $$$n$$$, $$$m$$$ and $$$w$$$ ($$$2 \le n, m \le 2 \cdot 10^3$$$, $$$1 \le w \le 10^9$$$), where $$$n$$$ and $$$m$$$ are city size, $$$w$$$ is time during which Dima moves between unoccupied cells. The next $$$n$$$ lines each contain $$$m$$$ numbers ($$$-1 \le a_{ij} \le 10^9$$$) — descriptions of cells. It is guaranteed that the cells $$$(1, 1)$$$ and $$$(n, m)$$$ are free.
output_specification: Output the minimum time it will take for Dima to get to school. If he cannot get to school at all, then output " -1 ".
approach_summary: Formulate the state transition graph with non-negative weights. Execute Dijkstra's algorithm with priority queue to find shortest paths in O((V + E) log V).

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1520G — To Go Or Not To Go? [168. Dijkstra's Algorithm]
topic_editorial.summary: Single-source shortest path using Dijkstra's algorithm.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: Because all edge weights are non-negative, the shortest distance to the unvisited vertex with the minimum tentative distance is finalized and cannot be decreased by further transitions (greedy choice property).
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Graph Modeling
Construct an adjacency list with pairs $(v, w)$ for each directed or undirected edge from $u$ to $v$ with weight $w \ge 0$.

### Step 2: Distance Table Initialization
Initialize $dist[v] = \infty$ for all vertices, with $dist[\text{source}] = 0$.
Push $(0, \text{source})$ into a min-priority queue `std::priority_queue<pair<long long, int>, vector<pair<long long, int>>, greater<>>`.

### Step 3: Relaxation Loop
While the priority queue is not empty:
1. Pop $(d, u)$. If $d > dist[u]$, discard (stale entry).
2. For each neighbor $(v, w)$ of $u$:
   If $dist[u] + w < dist[v]$:
   $$dist[v] = dist[u] + w$$
   Push $(dist[v], v)$ into the priority queue.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((V + E) \log V)$
  Every vertex is extracted from the priority queue at most once. For every edge, we perform at most one priority queue push operation taking $\mathcal{O}(\log V)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(V + E)$
  Required for storing the adjacency list and the distance array.
